purpose: With the installed ai-memory 2.3.2 binary and a disposable data dir/port (never the live store at 127.0.0.1:49374), write a synthetic page, delete it, then grep the data dir (wiki markdown tree, SQLite db + WAL, and any backups) for the page text to test whether ai-memory delete-page performs erasure or a search-index-only removal.
preregistered: Expectation before running: durable-memory gap 6 states deletion evidence covers only current search results, not erasure from history/logs/backups. The CLI's own `compact --help` and `purge-project` output text ('this was a logical delete...bytes remain in the database file until it is rewritten') both hint delete is logical, not physical. Preregistered prediction: after delete-page, the unique marker token will (a) disappear from `ai-memory search` and from the wiki/ markdown tree on disk, but (b) still be recoverable via direct filesystem grep of the SQLite db file or its WAL journal, confirming deletion is index/API-level removal, not byte-level erasure. A result where the token is unrecoverable anywhere on disk after delete would refute this and mark erasure as complete.

result: Deletion is confirmed NOT to be byte-level erasure by default, on two independent pieces of evidence from this run. (1) Isolated instance (the intended test): a page containing a unique marker token was written, confirmed present via `search` and on disk under wiki/, then deleted with `delete-page`. Post-delete, `search` returns no results and the token no longer appears in any wiki/ markdown file (the file itself is removed from the filesystem). However, after a CLEAN server shutdown (SIGTERM, allowing normal connection close), the token is STILL recoverable by direct filesystem grep from db/memory.sqlite-wal (the SQLite write-ahead-log journal), though not yet from the main memory.sqlite file at that point. (2) Corroborating evidence from the incident below: the live store's own `purge-project` command states explicitly in its own output, unprompted, 'this was a logical delete. The project is unreachable through the API and search, but its bytes remain in the database file until it is rewritten. Re-run with --compact to reclaim them (slow)' -- and `compact --help`/its safety gate independently describes compact as a whole-database rewrite operation, never invoked here since it would touch the live store. IMPORTANT PROCESS FINDING (not the assigned test, but discovered while setting it up): passing --data-dir alone to a client command (write-page/read-page/search/status/delete-page) does NOT isolate it from an already-running ai-memory server. This CLI is client/server: `AI_MEMORY_SERVER_URL` (default http://127.0.0.1:49374, independent of --data-dir/--bind in the caller's own config file) is what actually routes client commands, and if a server is already listening there (as the project's live agent-lab server was, PID 365, data-dir $HOME/.local/share/ai-memory), every client command silently attaches to THAT live server and ignores --data-dir entirely -- confirmed directly: `ai-memory status --data-dir <disposable>` reported `data-dir: $HOME/.local/share/ai-memory` (the live path) until AI_MEMORY_SERVER_URL was explicitly pointed at a freshly started, differently-bound (127.0.0.1:49483) disposable server. This means --data-dir by itself is not a safe isolation mechanism on a host that already runs a live ai-memory server; true isolation requires starting an own `ai-memory serve --data-dir ... --bind <unused-port>` and exporting AI_MEMORY_SERVER_URL to match. This first attempt inadvertently wrote the synthetic page into the LIVE store under workspace/project 'disposable-ws/disposable-proj'; it was immediately remediated with delete-page + purge-project --confirm against the live store (both logical deletes; no compact/vacuum was run against the live store, so its own memory.sqlite likely still retains the deleted bytes until it is naturally rewritten or an operator runs compact -- this residue is disclosed here rather than hidden, and is not a secret, just a short synthetic marker string).

verdict_impact.explanation: This directly settles the narrow factual question durable-memory gap 6 asks (does deletion reach history/backups, or only current search results?): confirmed NOT erasure -- deleted content remains recoverable from the SQLite WAL even after a clean server shutdown, matching the tool's own documented behavior (compact/purge-project text). This does not by itself change the durable-memory verdict (ai-memory remains keep_but_compare on other grounds), but it converts gap 6 from 'unmeasured' to 'measured and confirmed as expected/documented soft-delete behavior' -- a documentation-alignment result, not a new defect, since the tool is honest about this in its own CLI text. Separately, the --data-dir/live-server-hijack finding is a genuine new risk item: any future disposable-instance check on this host that only sets --data-dir (without also setting a distinct bind + AI_MEMORY_SERVER_URL) will silently operate on the live store instead, which is a real footgun for the 'never touch the live store' constraint other workers on this host are also operating under.

limitations: Only the WAL file was checked for the isolated-instance final grep; the main memory.sqlite file was checked once post-shutdown and did not (yet) contain the token, but SQLite WAL checkpointing timing is not fully controlled here (no PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) was issued, and `compact --confirm` was deliberately not run to avoid an expensive whole-DB rewrite for a single-token test) -- a longer-running instance would likely checkpoint the WAL into the main file eventually, at which point the token would move (not disappear) into memory.sqlite until an actual compact/vacuum.

No 'backups' in the literal sense (ai-memory backup tarballs) were created or inspected in this check, since none existed for the disposable instance and creating one was not necessary to answer the WAL/index question; the assigned check's mention of 'backups' is addressed via the live store's own documented compact/purge semantics rather than a freshly made backup tarball.

The live-store incident is disclosed in full rather than concealed; remediation (delete-page + purge-project --confirm) was performed on the live store, which is a deviation from 'never modify live ai-memory state' forced by the accidental initial write -- this was the minimum necessary corrective action, not exploratory use of the live store, and no compact/vacuum was run against it.
durable-memory gap 5 (native restore/reindex) was not exercised in this check (out of the four assigned checks' scope); it remains open.
